amendments.rule: **A verbless clause with a prepositional predicate takes its supplied copula on the preposition.** Rule 20 supplies the copula from the construction; where the predicate is a prepositional phrase, the copula joins the preposition heading that phrase and the unit heads on the preposition — `בְכַפֵּיהֶם` → *is in their hands*, `בִמְסִלּוֹתָם` → *are in their paths*, `אִתָּנוּ` → *are with us*, `עָלֶיךָ` → *is upon thee*. **And a modal or volitive auxiliary the ASV writes with that copula is part of it.** Where the clause carries jussive or optative force and the ASV writes *Let ... be*, *shall be*, *let there be* or another modal frame in the slot where the copula would stand, the whole frame is the construction-supplied copula and joins the preposition's unit, headed on the preposition as before, and no part of it is `added`: `רוֹמְמוֹת אֵל בִּגְרוֹנָם` → *Let the high praises of God* ***be in*** *their mouth* gives *Let ... be in* to the `בְּ`, discontinuous around the subject under rule 25, while the fronted construct nominal keeps its own English as the clause's subject. This is rule 17's ruling that a volitive frame belongs to the verb whose mood it renders, read for a clause that writes no verb for the frame to join, and rule 20's ruling that the copula is whatever verb the ASV writes where a copula would stand, read for the auxiliary written beside it; the directional case below already gives a modal *shall be* to the morpheme heading the predicate on the same terms. Do not divide such a frame, giving the *be* to the preposition and marking the *Let* `added` under rule 20's supplied-lexical-verb clause: what that clause governs is a verb introducing an event and a participant the Hebrew never wrote, as *were given* is, and a volitive auxiliary introduces neither. Read whether a verb stands in the clause before placing the word, since where one does rule 17 governs and the frame joins that verb; an ASV italic on the frame corroborates the supply and decides nothing, by rule 7. **A directional predicate whose relation is carried by a directive `he` rather than by a preposition is read on the same terms.** Rule 32 makes such a `he` its own aligned unit by rule 11 wherever the ASV writes a word of its own for it, so where that directional phrase is the predicate of a verbless clause the construction-supplied copula joins the `he`'s unit and that unit heads on the word written for the direction, discontinuous around the noun under rule 25: `דֶּגֶל מַחֲנֵה רְאוּבֵן תֵּימָנָה` → *On the south side shall be the standard of the camp of Reuben* gives *On … shall be* to the `he`, while `תֵּימָן` keeps *the south side*, headed on *south* under rule 31, and the construct chain keeps only its own English. Read the Hebrew for which side is the predicate, as this rule's closing paragraph and rule 20 both direct: a definite construct chain standing in such a clause is its subject, and the ASV's inversion of the English is not evidence against that. Two limits. Where the ASV writes no separate word for the `he` and the two share one unit under rule 30, there is no separate unit to carry the copula and it joins that one fused unit. And where a participial or other nominal phrase is the clause's subject, so that the directional phrase is not the predicate at all, rule 20 governs and the copula joins the nominal predicate instead — `וְהַחֹנִים קֵדְמָה מִזְרָחָה דֶּגֶל מַחֲנֵה יְהוּדָה` → *And those that encamp on the east side toward the sunrising shall be they of the standard of the camp of Judah* leaves the directive `he` its bare *on*. **A resultative prepositional predicate takes the ASV's supplied result or change frame on the same terms.** The preposition carries the relation that English expresses with the frame: `לְ` → *to be*, *shall be turned into*, *will be unto*, or *shalt become*. This is not rule 20's wholly supplied lexical verb, because removing the English frame removes the preposition's own result relation; any explicit Hebrew subject still takes the English subject pronoun separately. Head the preposition's unit on the English word carrying that relation — *to* in *to be*, *into* in *shall be turned into*, *unto* in *will be unto*, and *become* where no English preposition remains. The ordinary copular case is settled rather than a tie: the corpus reads it this way in 103 units across 39 chapters and never moves the copula onto the object noun instead. It is settled; the note need not hedge it. **A relational verb the ASV writes where a copula would stand goes the same way.** Where a possessive or belonging `לְ` heads the predicate and the ASV renders the clause with a verb of belonging rather than a bare copula — `אֲשֶׁר לַבָּיִת` → *which belonged to the house* — that verb is part of the preposition's own rendering and joins its unit, headed on the English preposition written for it. It is not rule 20's wholly supplied lexical verb: drop the verb and the preposition's relation is what has gone and nothing else, which is the subtraction test rule 43 applies to the same clause written with *had*. Where the ASV does write *had* or *have*, rule 43 governs; where it writes a bare copula, the first sentence of this rule does. **But every sentence above governs a phrase for which the ASV has written an English preposition, and says nothing about one for which it has written none.** Where the ASV spends no word on the preposition's own relation and instead writes that relation inside the following word — a possessive or belonging `לְ` rendered as an English genitive, `לַיהוָה` → *is Jehovah's* — rule 30's one-rendering condition is met: one English word carries both the relation and the lexeme, and the preposition shares that word's unit, headed on the word carrying the lexeme. The construction's copula then joins that one fused unit, exactly as it joins `לִפְנֵי` → *was before* under rule 30, which states that a copula the construction hands to the whole of an expression does not defeat the condition. Test by the subtraction rules 16, 30 and 43 use: drop the copula and ask whether the preposition has lost a rendering of its own or only the clause has lost the tense English writes for it. Where only the clause is diminished, the preposition has no separate English and fuses; where an English preposition of its own remains — *is in their hands* — the first sentence of this rule governs and the copula stays with it. Do not reach for rule 2 to split the fused pair on the ground that the noun or name holds an English word of its own: that reasoning is rule 57's, where each of two nouns holds a word, and here the preposition holds none. The corpus reads `לְ` + the divine name this way in six units across five chapters — *is Jehovah's*, *shall be Jehovah's*, *am Jehovah's*, and a bare *Jehovah's* — and never splits a copula onto the preposition beside a separately aligned name. **And every sentence above governs a preposition that is itself the clause's predicate, never one heading an adjunct the ASV has merely placed the copula beside.** Where a nominal predicate stands in the verbless clause and a prepositional phrase modifies it, the copula and any dummy subject are rule 20's and join that nominal, whichever order the ASV writes the two in: `חֻקַּת עוֹלָם לְדֹרֹתֵיכֶם` → *it shall be a statute for ever throughout your generations* and `מֵאֵת בְּנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּרִית עוֹלָם` → *it is on the behalf of the children of Israel an everlasting covenant* are one construction, and both give the copula to the construct nominal, the second unit discontinuous around the fronted phrase under rule 25 while the preposition keeps only the English written for its own relation. Read the Hebrew clause for which side is the predicate rather than the English word order, exactly as rule 20 directs, since a phrase the ASV fronts puts the copula beside something that predicates nothing; and do not let a fused compound preposition draw the copula in under rule 30's one-rendering condition, which reaches a copula the construction hands to that expression and not one another morpheme is there to take. Where the clause writes no nominal predicate at all, nothing competes and the first sentence of this rule governs as before. **But a nominal standing beside a prepositional phrase is not a nominal predicate merely because the ASV writes the copula next to it.** Where the clause writes no subject but that one nominal, and the ASV writes no separate English subject for the clause either, the nominal is the clause's subject and the prepositional phrase is its predicate, so the copula stays on the preposition under this rule's first sentence — whichever order the ASV writes the two in, and however indefinite the English nominal is. `בְּפֶשַׁע שְׂפָתַיִם מוֹקֵשׁ רָע` → *In the transgression of the lips* ***is*** *a snare*, `בְּאֹרַח־צְדָקָה חַיִּים` → *In the way of righteousness* ***is*** *life*, `מִרְמָה בְּלֶב־חֹרְשֵׁי רָע` → *Deceit* ***is in*** *the heart of them that devise evil* and `וּלְיֹעֲצֵי שָׁלוֹם שִׂמְחָה` → *But* ***to*** *the counsellors of peace* ***is*** *joy* all put the copula on the preposition, and an indefinite *a snare* is no more a predicate than the definite construct chain the paragraph above calls a subject. What the preceding paragraph governs is a clause that has a subject of its own for the nominal to predicate of, which the ASV writes as a separate English subject — the *it* of *it shall be a statute for ever throughout your generations* and of *it is on the behalf of the children of Israel an everlasting covenant* — and a nominal that is itself the English subject of the copula in question is not that. So count the clause's nominals against the subjects the ASV writes, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s, before reading a phrase as an adjunct: where the only candidate subject is the nominal beside the preposition, the prepositional phrase is what predicates of it.
amendments.why: PSA.149.6 renders a verbless clause with a prepositional predicate by a volitive frame — `רוֹמְמוֹת אֵל בִּגְרוֹנָם` → *Let the high praises of God be in their mouth*, both frame words italicized. Rule 49 already sends the construction-supplied copula to the preposition and rule 49's own directional example already gives a modal *shall be* there, but nothing in the contract said where the *Let* goes, and rule 20's supplied-lexical-verb clause is close enough to tempt a pass into splitting the frame and marking *Let* `added`. The amendment states the whole frame is the copula, cites the rules it rests on (17 for the volitive frame, 20 for the copula being whatever verb stands in that slot), and marks the boundary against rule 20's supplied lexical verb by the test that rule itself gives — a volitive auxiliary introduces no event and no participant the Hebrew did not write. The corpus supports rather than contradicts it: `בְּ` carries the construction-supplied copula in 143 *is in*, 68 *are in*, 59 *was in* and 57 *were in* units, always headed on the preposition, and a modal or volitive form of that same copula is the same construction. Placed inside rule 49 rather than as a new rule so the qualification stands where a pass reading the copula sentence will meet it, and the rest of rule 49 is returned unchanged.

conventions: A volitive 'Let' the ASV writes for a Hebrew jussive or for a verbless clause with jussive force is never added in this chapter, and where it goes depends on whether a verb stands. In PSA.149.2, .3 and .5 a jussive verb stands and the frame joins that verb under rule 17, discontinuous around the subject under rule 25. In PSA.149.6 the clause is verbless with a prepositional predicate and no verb stands, so the whole supplied 'Let ... be' is the construction-supplied copula and joins the preposition under rule 49, headed on the preposition; the fronted construct nominal is the clause's subject and takes none of it, and the ASV's italics on 'Let' and 'be' corroborate the supply without deciding it, by rule 7.

The chapter supplies a definite article twice inside one anarthrous construct chain. In PSA.149.1 'in the assembly of the saints' no article morpheme stands anywhere in the phrase: the construct noun takes the first supplied 'the' under rule 29 and the substantival adjective serving as rectum takes the second under rule 46, alongside the relational 'of' rule 19 gives it. The bare substantival 'the' stands alone in PSA.149.4 'the meek' and PSA.149.5 'the saints', and is supplied nowhere in PSA.149.9, where the written suffix's possessive already determines the phrase. Two supplied 'the's in one anarthrous chain are not evidence of a fronted article.

Verbs of singing head on 'sing', not on the noun or adverbial beside it: zamar 'Let them sing praises' (PSA.149.3) and ranan 'Let them sing for joy' (PSA.149.5) both head on the verb, because rule 31's subtraction leaves 'praises' and 'for joy' naming no singing while 'sing' still writes the making of music and the vocal cry. Verbs whose English is a true light verb with a complement head the other way under rule 44 - gil 'be joyful' on 'joyful' (PSA.149.2), ratsah 'taketh pleasure' on 'pleasure' (PSA.149.4). Each verse note names the competing reading.

PSA.149.7 bal is a divergence the pipeline has recorded no textual decision for. MACULA segments the word as the negative particle bal followed by ummim, while the ASV read balumim as a pointed preposition with its article on leom and wrote 'upon the'. The packet marks no variant unit in that slot, so rule 53's second paragraph governs: the English is aligned as printed to the token the projection carries, on the terms the construction would otherwise take, headed on the relational word under rule 24. Do not mark the token unrepresented and the English added, and do not take a new textual decision in the alignment file, which rule 9 forbids.

The corpus reads `לְ` + the divine name this way in six units across five chapters — *is Jehovah's*, *shall be Jehovah's*, *am Jehovah's*, and a bare *Jehovah's* — and never splits a copula onto the preposition beside a separately aligned name. **And every sentence above governs a preposition that is itself the clause's predicate, never one heading an adjunct the ASV has merely placed the copula beside.** Where a nominal predicate stands in the verbless clause and a prepositional phrase modifies it, the copula and any dummy subject are rule 20's and join that nominal, whichever order the ASV writes the two in: `חֻקַּת עוֹלָם לְדֹרֹתֵיכֶם` → *it shall be a statute for ever throughout your generations* and `מֵאֵת בְּנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּרִית עוֹלָם` → *it is on the behalf of the children of Israel an everlasting covenant* are one construction, and both give the copula to the construct nominal, the second unit discontinuous around the fronted phrase under rule 25 while the preposition keeps only the English written for its own relation. Read the Hebrew clause for which side is the predicate rather than the English word order, exactly as rule 20 directs, since a phrase the ASV fronts puts the copula beside something that predicates nothing; and do not let a fused compound preposition draw the copula in under rule 30's one-rendering condition, which reaches a copula the construction hands to that expression and not one another morpheme is there to take. Where the clause writes no nominal predicate at all, nothing competes and the first sentence of this rule governs as before. **But a nominal standing beside a prepositional phrase is not a nominal predicate merely because the ASV writes the copula next to it.** Where the clause writes no subject but that one nominal, and the ASV writes no separate English subject for the clause either, the nominal is the clause's subject and the prepositional phrase is its predicate, so the copula stays on the preposition under this rule's first sentence — whichever order the ASV writes the two in, and however indefinite the English nominal is. `בְּפֶשַׁע שְׂפָתַיִם מוֹקֵשׁ רָע` → *In the transgression of the lips* ***is*** *a snare*, `בְּאֹרַח־צְדָקָה חַיִּים` → *In the way of righteousness* ***is*** *life*, `מִרְמָה בְּלֶב־חֹרְשֵׁי רָע` → *Deceit* ***is in*** *the heart of them that devise evil* and `וּלְיֹעֲצֵי שָׁלוֹם שִׂמְחָה` → *But* ***to*** *the counsellors of peace* ***is*** *joy* all put the copula on the preposition, and an indefinite *a snare* is no more a predicate than the definite construct chain the paragraph above calls a subject. What the preceding paragraph governs is a clause that has a subject of its own for the nominal to predicate of, which the ASV writes as a separate English subject — the *it* of *it shall be a statute for ever throughout your generations* and of *it is on the behalf of the children of Israel an everlasting covenant* — and a nominal that is itself the English subject of the copula in question is not that. So count the clause's nominals against the subjects the ASV writes, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s, before reading a phrase as an adjunct: where the only candidate subject is the nominal beside the preposition, the prepositional phrase is what predicates of it.
amended.why: PSA.149.6 renders a verbless clause with a prepositional predicate by a volitive frame — `רוֹמְמוֹת אֵל בִּגְרוֹנָם` → *Let the high praises of God be in their mouth*, both frame words italicized. Rule 49 already sends the construction-supplied copula to the preposition and rule 49's own directional example already gives a modal *shall be* there, but nothing in the contract said where the *Let* goes, and rule 20's supplied-lexical-verb clause is close enough to tempt a pass into splitting the frame and marking *Let* `added`. The amendment states the whole frame is the copula, cites the rules it rests on (17 for the volitive frame, 20 for the copula being whatever verb stands in that slot), and marks the boundary against rule 20's supplied lexical verb by the test that rule itself gives — a volitive auxiliary introduces no event and no participant the Hebrew did not write. The corpus supports rather than contradicts it: `בְּ` carries the construction-supplied copula in 143 *is in*, 68 *are in*, 59 *was in* and 57 *were in* units, always headed on the preposition, and a modal or volitive form of that same copula is the same construction. Placed inside rule 49 rather than as a new rule so the qualification stands where a pass reading the copula sentence will meet it, and the rest of rule 49 is returned unchanged.

report: All eight candidate lemmas checked; none is a split. Each difference is licensed by the ASV's own wording or by the source context: the preposition alternates in/with/upon on what the ASV wrote (PSA.149.3 writes both 'in the dance' and 'with timbrel' in one verse); lamed is 'To' before an infinitive construct (vv.7-9, rule 52), 'unto' before a name or a suffix (vv.1, 3), and 'have' on the possessive predicate (v9, rule 43); halal differs only as imperative against jussive; hasid stands bare (v5), as a construct chain's rectum (v1), and under a written possessive (v9).

The candidate table is blind to added units, so I read the dump end to end for supplied English. Two supplied 'And's (PSA.149.1 t010, PSA.149.7 t007) open cola in which no conjunction morpheme stands and are added; the three written waws (vv.3, 6, 8) each take the connective the ASV wrote. Rule 14's count is run identically in every colon, and no supplied coordinator is folded into a neighbouring noun anywhere in the chapter.

The four volitive 'Let's are placed by one principle and none is added: on the jussive verb in vv.2, 3 and 5 under rule 17, and on the preposition heading the prepositional predicate in v6 under rule 49, that clause writing no verb for the frame to join. This is the one judgment the contract did not state outright, and it is the basis of the amendment below.

Supplied determiners are consistent: rule 29 on a construct noun (vv.1, 2, 6), rule 46 on an anarthrous substantive (vv.1, 4, 5), rule 15 on a plain noun (vv.3, 9), and none in v9, where the written suffix's possessive already determines the phrase. PSA.149.1 writes two supplied 'the's inside one anarthrous chain and gives each to the rule that licenses it - the construct takes one, the substantival rectum the other - rather than reading the second as a fronted article.

Head choices on the singing verbs were reviewed against the light-verb heads and the line holds: zamar 'sing praises' (v3) and ranan 'sing for joy' (v5) head on 'sing', where rule 31's subtraction leaves the complement naming nothing, while gil 'be joyful' (v2) and ratsah 'taketh pleasure' (v4) head on the complement under rule 44, where the English verb is a true light verb. Both verse notes name the competing reading, as rule 8 requires.

PSA.149.7 bal: the ASV read balumim as preposition plus article plus leom and wrote 'upon the'; the packet records no variant unit in that slot, so rule 53's unmarked-divergence paragraph governs and the verse pass aligned the English as printed against the token the projection carries, headed on 'upon'. That is what the contract directs, and marking the token unrepresented with the English added would have been the error. No patch.
BSB reports 96/96 comparable source occurrences in agreement and lists no disagreements, so there is nothing to adjudicate and no aggregate score was consulted in any judgment above.
No patches. Four conventions recorded for judgments the report showed reaching later verses unlogged, and one amendment to rule 49 for the volitive copula.
